title: Learning is Wealth—Wilson, Charley, Rebecca, and Rosa, Slaves from New Orleans
medium: Albumen silver print from glass negative
credit: The Horace W. Goldsmith Foundation Fund, through Joyce and Robert Menschel, 2011
caption_tea: Charles Paxson's studio portrait of formerly enslaved children and an adult man was sold as a carte de visite captioned "Learning is Wealth," part of an 1863-64 fundraising campaign that used photographs of children posed with schoolbooks to solicit donations for freedpeople's education in Union-occupied Louisiana.
caption_basic: Learning is Wealth—Wilson, Charley, Rebecca, and Rosa, Slaves from New Orleans by Charles Paxson (1863–64) -- Albumen silver print from glass negative

tea_voice_claims.text: The Library of Congress records this carte de visite by Charles Paxson of New York, entered for copyright in 1864, and notes that the net proceeds from sale of the photographs were devoted to the education of freedpeople in the Department of the Gulf
The sitters are Wilson Chinn, Charles Taylor, Rebecca Huger and Rosina Downs, photographed with schoolbooks for the caption "Learning is Wealth"

cast.name: Wilson Chinn
cast.tidbit: Formerly enslaved on a Louisiana plantation, Wilson Chinn was one of the adults who toured the North with these children as part of an 1863-64 campaign, appearing in a separate, widely reproduced photograph that documented the branding iron and shackles used on enslaved people.
cast.role_in_scene: Seated at left with a book

cast.name: Charles "Charley" Taylor
cast.tidbit: Despite a complexion light enough that Union sympathizers used his photograph to argue slavery could ensnare people who looked white, Charley had been sold twice -- first by his own father and enslaver, Alexander Wethers of Virginia, to a trader who sold him on to a New Orleans owner.

cast.name: Rebecca Huger
cast.tidbit: Rebecca had been enslaved as her own father's household attendant to a girl only slightly older than herself; contemporary accounts noted that in the few months since her emancipation she had already learned to read and write.

cast.name: Rosina "Rosa" Downs
cast.tidbit: The youngest of the four, Rosa was photographed and toured alongside the others specifically because -- like Rebecca and Charley -- her fair complexion was used to unsettle Northern audiences into recognizing enslaved children as no different from their own.
cast.role_in_scene: Seated with a book, not quite 7 years old

cast_context.text: Brought north from Union-occupied Louisiana by Colonel George H. Hanks in 1863-64, these four formerly enslaved children and several adults toured Northern cities and were photographed to raise funds for the first schools for freedpeople in the Department of the Gulf -- Harper's Weekly ran engravings of the photographs alongside their biographies to fuel the campaign.

findings.message: Photograph of enslaved and emancipated people -- not material this collection should present as a relaxing browse.

title: Heroic Head of Pierre de Wissant, One of the Burghers of Calais
caption_tea: In 1347, after a year-long siege, England's Edward III agreed to spare the French city of Calais on one condition: six of its leading citizens had to walk out barefoot, nooses around their necks, and surrender themselves for execution. Pierre de Wissant was one of them. More than five centuries later, Rodin sculpted each burgher not as a stoic martyr but caught mid-feeling — dread, resignation, defiance — and this bronze head isolates de Wissant's face at that exact pitch of emotion.
caption_basic: Heroic Head of Pierre de Wissant, One of the Burghers of Calais by Auguste Rodin (1886) -- bronze

tea_voice_claims.text: In 1347, after a year's siege, six citizens of Calais surrendered themselves to Edward III of England, barefoot and in nooses, in exchange for sparing the city — recorded in Jean Froissart's Chronicles.
Rodin depicted each of the six burghers, including Pierre de Wissant, expressing distinct emotions — despair, resignation, courage, uncertainty — rather than uniform heroism.

title: And I Saw in the Right Hand of Him that Sat on the Throne a Book Written within and on the Backside, Sealed with Seven Seals
caption_tea: The whole plot turns on this one object: a scroll sealed seven times, held by the figure on the throne. An angel calls out asking who is worthy to open it, and the answer is nobody — John writes that he 'wept much' because no one could be found. Then an elder tells him to stop crying, because someone has been found after all. Everything that follows in the book is what happens when those seals come off.
caption_basic: And I Saw in the Right Hand of Him that Sat on the Throne a Book Written within and on the Backside, Sealed with Seven Seals by Odilon Redon (1899) -- lithograph

tea_voice_claims.text: Rev 5:1-2: a book sealed with seven seals in the right hand of him that sat on the throne, and an angel asking who is worthy to open it
Rev 5:4: 'And I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book'
The opening of the seven seals marks the beginning of the apocalypse in Revelation
